sweep_summary: Jamaican Creole (jama1262) is in the catalog as weight-hedged (leftmost heavy syllable, default penultimate, trochaic; heavy = CVV/CVC), deciding source Gooden 2007 ICPhS-satellite workshop paper. Four title-works with stress in the title, all unlisted: (1) Gooden 2003 'Prosodic contrast in JC reduplication' (De Gruyter, paywalled: WAF challenge, no OA copy) and (4) Gooden 2007 'Morphophonological properties of pitch accents in JC reduplication' (Benjamins CLL 32, paywalled: not reachable by automated download, Semantic Scholar CLOSED) are both about JC stress/pitch accent in reduplication and are the published spin-offs of Gooden's 2003 OSU thesis; priority medium, but the thesis they rest on is. (3) Gooden 2003 Battlebridge chapter 'Semantic functions and prosodic constraints' has no digital edition anywhere found (print only, low priority). (2) Lacoste 2021 'Variation in stress in the Jamaican classroom' (Benjamins, abstract read via Crossref) is a sociophonetic study of Standard Jamaican English classroom speech (exaggerated stress correlates on word-final syllables) and is silent on JC stress placement. Best statement actually read: Gooden's 2003 thesis, ch. 5, sec. 5.3 p.3% LLH exception class (p. 161) -- confirms and refines the catalog's classification, and as the primary full analysis to which the 2007 workshop paper itself defers ('see Gooden 2003 for a detailed analysis') it should replace the workshop paper as the deciding source; the 'hedged' coding stands. Side note from the held Harry 2006 JIPA illustration (p. 129): 'there is no consensus on the nature of the prosodic/intonational patterns in Jamaican Creole' -- Devonish & Harry 2004 analyse JC as a mixed stress-tone system, a caution for the catalog's tone field. all lookups went through DOI/Crossref/Semantic Scholar/archive.org/the Internet Archive (the Internet Archive became unreachable partway through).

new_statements.quote: As we have seen, in monomorphemic words primary stress generally falls on the leftmost heavy syllable. If there is no heavy syllable, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable of a word. Secondary stress falls two syllables away from the syllable with primary stress, if there is such a syllable except in the case of word final light syllables which do not bear stress. In the majority of cases, stress falls on the initial or penultimate syllable of a word and falls only rarely on the final syllable. Where secondary stress falls on a word final syllable it is typically a heavy syllable. These patterns are reflective of the general pattern for 90% of the words in the database.

PhD thesis, The Ohio State University (Columbus), xxiv+297 pp. Chapter 5 'Word Level Stress in Jamaican Creole', pp. 151-195. new_statements.reading: First-hand, data-based statement (database drawn from Cassidy & LePage's Dictionary of Jamaican English acute-accent marks cross-checked against native-speaker prominence judgments, p. 151-152). Rule: weight-sensitive, trochaic; primary stress on the leftmost (or only) heavy syllable, heavy = long vowel, diphthong or coda consonant with no superheavy distinction (p. 85); default penultimate when no heavy syllable; secondary stress two syllables from the primary but never on a final light syllable; compounds take main stress on the rightmost member (p. 168). Quantified hedging: the general pattern covers 90% of the database; 8.3% of trisyllables are LLH with initial primary and final secondary stress (p. 161); other alternate-pattern words are 'predominantly' penultimate regardless of weight (p. 162). This CONFIRMS the catalog's classification (weight-hedged; unbounded leftmost-heavy, default penultimate, CVV+CVC heavy) and REFINES it with the 90% / 8.3% figures and the exception classes. Already held by the project from the 2026-09-16 download pass; read in full this search of works with stress in the title.

new_statements.quote: (16) If there is a heavy syllable in one of either the first or second syllables of a word, primary stress falls on the first heavy syllable from the left. In the absence of heavy syllables, primary stress falls on the first syllable. [...] (17) Secondary stress falls on the third syllable of a trisyllabic word if it is heavy. (No stress is assigned to a final, third syllable if it is light, as in 16D above). In four syllable words in which all the syllables are light (primary stress falls on the first syllable, and) secondary stress falls on the third syllable. [...] There are also a large body of data where the left word level prominence generalization is actually reversed: primary stress is sometimes assigned to the rightmost heavy syllable, or the first of two word-final light syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Gooden 2003 statement on the type (weight-sensitive, trochaic, primary stress on the leftmost heavy syllable; heavy = CVV, diphthong, CVC) and on secondary stress never landing on a final light syllable. It DIFFERS on the default when no syllable is heavy: Alderete (16) puts primary stress on the FIRST syllable (krákasa, áfrikan, mógikl, ínikwìti, bániklèva — left-to-right footing), whereas Gooden 2003 puts it on the PENULTIMATE syllable ('If there is no heavy syllable, primary stress falls on the penultimate syllable'). The two coincide for disyllables and diverge for words of three or more light syllables; both are analyses of the same Cassidy & LePage dictionary…
new_statements.rule_in_words: weight-sensitive, trochaic, left-to-right: primary stress on the leftmost heavy syllable (heavy = long vowel, diphthong, or short vowel plus coda consonant; p. 11: 'long vowels, diphthongs, and short vowel plus consonant sequences count as heavy syllables in JC'), and in words with no heavy syllable on the first syllable (éda, krákasa 'fan palm', áfrikan; p. 12-13: 'Trisyllabic forms such as krákasa suggest that stress assignment moves from left to right because stress falls on the first syllable'). In H L L words the penult is stressed (sàNkúku), which the author takes as the moraic-trochee footing (sàN)(kúku) (p. 13). The author's own analytic conclusion: the JC foot is a moraic trochee (sec. 3.4, p. 13). Data are the accent marks of Cassidy & LePage 1980 (Dictionary of Jamaican English).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Rule (17), p. 11: secondary stress on a heavy final third syllable of a trisyllable (búosifài, báabikyùu, frúutapàN, báNgaràm); none on a final light syllable; in four-syllable all-light words on the third syllable (ínikwìti, bániklèva, álikàša). p. 12: 'Sometimes the first stress peak in a word is not louder than the second peak' (kókomáka, jérimáia). Iteratives: báta báta, sági sàgi.
new_statements.exceptions: p. 12, (18) 'Final Primary Stress': 'a large body of data' with the generalization reversed — primary stress on the rightmost heavy syllable or on the first of two word-final light syllables: bàgabú 'insects', kàrató (L L L), èbeláit, kàkabán (L L H), kàkifíeva (L L H L), sàNkúku, stàarápl (compound), sàNkóco (H L L), àianái 'Rastafarian', gàNgalú, pùotagíi 'Portuguese' (H L H); the author calls the left/right variation 'a loose interpretation of this parameter' (p. 13). Footnote 9 (p. 11): 'The assignment of stress in JC is not always perceptable. That is, the relative prominence of syllables is often quite level in rapid connected speech. Cassidy & LePage 1980 suggest that this fact is due to the influence on JC from West African tone languages such as Twi (p. xliv). Peter Patrick (personal communication) speculates that what is perceived as JC "stress" is really a unique compounding of three factors: loudness, pitch, and length.' Also p. 11: 'I have no independent evidence, aside from the iterative data, supporting this claim' (about the heavy-syllable inventory).
new_statements.identity_note: Both readable sources describe general Jamaican Creole (basilectal/mesolectal lexicon as recorded in Cassidy & LePage's Dictionary of Jamaican English); no particular dialect is singled out. Work 1's PuRe metadata (Colchester: Univ. of Essex, 47 pp., dated 2003, external file on Peter Patrick's Essex site) matches Peter L. Patrick's manuscript 'Jamaican Creole: morphology and syntax' (published 2004 in Kortmann et al., A Handbook of Varieties of English II, 407-438; DOI 10.1515/9783110208405.2.609; Essex repository record 11700), not a work by Beryl Bailey; the record's internal file name points instead to Bailey 1966, Jamaican Creole Syntax (Cambridge UP). The catalog entry's author attribution is therefore a PuRe/Glottolog cataloguing error.

readall_conflicts: Alderete 1993 (sec. 3.3, rule (16), preprint p. 11) and Gooden 2003 (existing statement) agree that Jamaican Creole word stress is weight-sensitive and trochaic with primary stress on the leftmost heavy syllable (heavy = long vowel, diphthong, closed syllable), and that no stress falls on a final light syllable. They disagree on the default in words with no heavy syllable: Alderete places primary stress on the FIRST syllable with left-to-right foot construction (krákasa 'fan palm', áfrikan, mógikl; four-syllable ínikwìti, bániklèva), while Gooden places it on the PENULTIMATE syllable. The two rules coincide on disyllables and diverge on words of three or more light syllables; both are analyses of the accent marks in Cassidy & LePage's Dictionary of Jamaican English. Alderete also reports 'a large body of data' with reversed, right-edge prominence (final stress in bàgabú, kàrató; penultimate in H L L sàNkúku) which he calls 'a loose interpretation of this parameter' (p. 13), and notes (fn. 9) that prominence is often nearly level in connected speech and, per Peter Patrick, may be a compound of loudness, pitch and length; Harry 2006 (JIPA, already held) likewise reports no consensus on word prosody. The Bailey/Patrick item could not be opened and adds nothing.
